# SK3061 — The `lock` target is not the object other threads take

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A `lock` taken over an object created in the same invocation, or over a field the type reassigns, so the monitor it takes is not the monitor another thread takes.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Async |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Compilation |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S2445, S6507 |

## Why

A `lock` excludes exactly the threads that take the same monitor, and the monitor lives on the object — so which object it is, is the entire contract. Both shapes here break it in the same way and read as correct: a local initialized with `new` gives every invocation its own monitor, so the critical section excludes nobody and the whole construct is a no-op; a field the type reassigns gives whoever entered before the reassignment a different monitor from whoever enters after, so two threads sit inside the same `lock` body at the same time. ⚠ **Neither produces a symptom that points at the lock.** The code compiles, the critical section is right there in the file, and the corruption it was supposed to prevent shows up as a data bug somewhere else.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Meter {
    int count;

    public void Bump() {
        var gate = new object();   // a new monitor every call; this excludes nobody

        lock (gate) {
            count++;
        }
    }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Meter {
    readonly Lock gate = new();

    int count;

    public void Bump() {
        lock (gate) {
            count++;
        }
    }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Fixless.** Introducing a shared lock object changes the type's shape and hoisting the local to a field changes its lifetime; which one is meant depends on what the type is for, and the `lock` statement does not say. ⚠ **The weak-identity types are `CA2002`'s and are excluded before either shape — measured, not assumed.** On a pristine `net10.0` class library with empty `Directory.Build.props`/`.targets` above it, one shape per file, `CA2002` fires on `lock (this)`, `lock (typeof(T))`, a string literal, a `string` field and `Thread.CurrentThread`, and is **silent** on a fresh local, a `readonly object` field and a mutable `object` field — which is the whole of both shapes this rule does report. ⚠ **Shape 2 used to ask whether a field was mutable and never what type it was, so a private `string` gate reassigned outside a constructor carried both findings** (#307). Re-probed: `CA2002` also fires on a `string` *local*, on a `Thread` field and on a `MemberInfo` field, so the overlap was wider than one clause in the field shape — `String`, `MarshalByRefObject`, `MemberInfo`, `ParameterInfo` and `Thread` are now excluded on the lock target's type, up the base chain, before shape 1 or shape 2 is consulted. `ExecutionEngineException`, `OutOfMemoryException` and `StackOverflowException` are on `CA2002`'s list and left off this one: nobody locks them, and every name here is recall given up. ⚠ Its shipped descriptor is `IsEnabledByDefault=False, DefaultSeverity=Warning`, listed only in `analysislevel_10_all.globalconfig`, so it is invisible in an ordinary build **and visible in Skala's own repository, which raises `AnalysisMode`** — which is precisely why duplicating it would double-report here first. The silences in that measurement are instrument-checked: the same file produced five `CA2002` findings once the severity was raised. ⚠ **Shape 1's load-bearing clause is that only an object *creation* counts.** `var gate = this.gate;` and `var gate = Shared.Gate;` alias an object other threads take and are correct; they are the single most likely false positive and they have a fixture each. The local must also never be reassigned and never be captured by a lambda — a delegate that closes over it gives it a lifetime longer than the invocation, and the "one monitor per call" argument stops holding. ⚠ **Shape 2 requires a *private* field assigned outside a constructor.** Private is what makes the analysis complete rather than a guess: every write is then inside the type. A field assigned only in a constructor or only in its initializer is effectively `readonly`, is common, is correct, and has two fixtures holding it. ⚠ **`SK3040`'s types are declined in both shapes.** `var s = new SemaphoreSlim(1); lock (s) { }` is a fresh local *and* a lock over a synchronization primitive, and the second reading is the one that tells the reader what to do. ⚠ **`SK1023` is disjoint by construction rather than by filter**: it modernizes a `lock` over a *private readonly* `object` field, and shape 2 requires a field that is not `readonly`, so no field can carry both findings. ⚠ **A `lock` in a top-level program is examined, and used not to be** (#307). The synthesized `Program` type declares itself at the *compilation unit* rather than at a type declaration, so an `OfType<TypeDeclarationSyntax>()` filter dropped the whole file in silence; 'a top-level statement file is a script rather than a shared-state type' was the wrong reading of that fact, because a top-level program is the shape a model writes first. ⚠ **`SK3060` is blind to the same file and this did not repair it** — measured, not read: three locks in a top-level program draw `SK3040` and `SK3061`, and the same source inside a class draws `SK3040`, `SK3060` and `SK3061`. `SK3060` declines through its own `Body` walk, which returns null at a type declaration and is what makes a field initializer decline too. ⚠ **`SK3044`'s gap is empty**: it reports on a field, top-level statements declare only locals, and a type declared beside them has a real type declaration.
